summary: One of the set of documents describing the Internet Printing Protocol (IPP), an application-level protocol for distributed printing. This one sets out requirements for notifications in IPP.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3997 is a requirements document for the notification part of the Internet Printing Protocol. It says who may ask to be told about a print job, which changes to a job or a printer count as events, how the notification is delivered, and what has to be true of a subscriber before a printer accepts the request.

subtitle: What has to happen when a print job changes state and somebody has to be told.

tldr.problem: A print job that is submitted over the network can finish, stall or fail while the person who sent it is somewhere else, and there was no agreed way to say who gets told about it or how the message reaches them.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the terms a notification service needs, walks through twelve situations in which notifications are wanted, and lists seventeen requirements for the specification that would follow: who may subscribe, to which events, with which attributes, and by which delivery method.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo that sets requirements for a separate specification, RFC 3995, which covers the event notifications and subscriptions themselves.

facts.label: Authors
facts.value: Tom Hastings, Roger deBry and Harry Lewis

today: RFC 3997 is an Informational memo published in March 2005, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It states requirements for the notification part of IPP, which RFC 3995 then went on to specify.

sections.title: What IPP Notifications Are For
sections.content:
The Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) is an application-level protocol that can be used for distributed printing on the Internet. There are multiple parts to IPP, but the primary architectural components are the Model, the Protocol, and an interface to Directory Services. RFC 3997 provides a statement of the requirements for notifications as an optional part of an IPP Service.

The scope of the requirements document covers functionality used by three kinds of IPP users: End Users, Print Administrators, and Operators. The extensions to the Internet Printing Protocol versions 1.0 and 1.1 are described in RFC 3995, and the base set of IPP documents is listed in the appendix to this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: IPP is the protocol that lets a program send a print job to a printer over the network and ask it what is happening. This memo covers the notification half of that: the part where a printer tells somebody that a job has changed state.

sections.title: The Vocabulary of Notifications
sections.content:
The memo defines the people and the parts. A Job-Submitting End User is a human end user who submits a print job to an IPP Printer, and who may or may not be in the same security domain as the printer and may or may not be geographically near it. An Administrator is a human user who established policy for and configures the print system, and an Operator is a human user who carries out that policy and controls the day-to-day running of the print system. A Job-Submitting Application, for example a batch application, acts on behalf of a Job-Submitting End User and submits a print job to an IPP Printer. A Security Domain is the set of network components that can communicate without going through a proxy or firewall, and it may be geographically very large. An IPP Client is the software component that sends IPP requests to an IPP Printer object and accepts IPP responses from it.

The people on the receiving side of a print job have their own names. The Job Recipient is the human who is the ultimate consumer of the print job, which in many cases is the same person as the Job-Submitting End User but need not be: if you print a document on a printer in a business partner's office, you are the Job-Submitting End User and the person the document is intended for is the Job Recipient. A Job Recipient Proxy acts on behalf of the Job Recipient and physically picks up the printed document from the printer if the Job Recipient cannot do so, so by definition the proxy is geographically near the printer and in the same security domain as it.

The notification machinery has four named parts. A Notification Subscriber is a client that requests the IPP Printer to send Event Notifications to one or more Notification Recipients, and may be a Job-Submitting End User or an End User, Operator, or Administrator that is not submitting a job. The Notification Source is the entity that sends Event Notifications. A Notification Recipient is the entity that receives IPP Notifications about Job and/or Printer events, and may be a Job-Submitting End User, a Job-Submitting Application, a Job Recipient, a Job Recipient Proxy, an Operator, an Administrator, or their representative, log file, usage statistics-gathering application, or other active or passive entity. A Notification Recipient Agent is a program that receives Event Notifications on behalf of the Notification Recipient, and may take action on the recipient's behalf, forward the notification by some alternative means such as paging the recipient, or queue it for later retrieval.

An Event is an occurrence, expected or unexpected, within the printing system of a change of state, condition, or configuration of a Job or Printer object. When an event occurs, an Event Notification is generated that fully describes it, including what the event was, where it occurred and when it occurred. Event Notifications are delivered to all the Notification Recipients that are subscribed to that Event, if any, using the delivery method defined in the subscription. An Event Notification is sent only if there is a corresponding subscription, and a Notification Subscription is the request by a Notification Subscriber to have Event Notifications sent to specified Notification Recipients when an event occurs.

Subscriptions can ask for extra detail. IPP Objects from which notifications are sent may have associated attributes, and a user may want one or more of these returned along with a particular notification. The examples the memo lists include number-of-intervening jobs, job-k-octets, job impressions, job-state-reasons, Job ID, Printer URI, and Subscription ID for a job-independent subscription.

How the notification is delivered is described by a Notification Delivery Method, of which email is one example. An Immediate Notification is sent so that it arrives immediately, within the limits of common addressing, routing, network congestion and quality of service. A Store-and-Forward Notification is not necessarily delivered immediately but is queued for delivery by an intermediate network application, for later retrieval; email is an example of that. Reliable Delivery of Notifications means delivery over a reliable transport with acknowledgement and retry, so that delivery is guaranteed within determinate time limits. The memo points out that guaranteed delivery requires both a store-and-forward notification and a reliable transport, because if the recipient has logged off and gone home an immediate notification cannot be guaranteed even over a reliable transport, since there is nothing there to catch it. A Notification over Unreliable Transport is delivered through the fundamental transport and routing framework with no acknowledgement or retry required, and any process-to-process communication involved is unconstrained.

Finally, a Human-Consumable Notification is intended for human end users only, a Machine-Consumable Notification is intended for consumption by a program only, such as an IPP Client, and may not contain human-readable information, and a Mixed Notification contains both. Machine-readable notifications are intended for application-to-application use, and the Notification Recipient could process one into human-readable form.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo names every part of the arrangement. You have the person who sends the job, the person who collects it, the printer that does the work, the program that asked to be told, and the program that receives the message on the recipient's behalf. An event is any change in the state of a job or a printer, and a notification is the message that describes it.

sections.title: Scenarios
sections.content:
The memo works through twelve situations in which notifications are wanted, each stated as a person and a list of subscription attributes.

In the first scenario, someone in the office submits a job to the printer down the hall and wants to know immediately when it will be completed, or if there is a problem, because the document is urgent. The subscription names the submitter as the Notification Recipient, all events, the job-state-reason attribute, and the Immediate notification type. In the second, the same person works from home and cannot collect the output, so they would like their secretary to pick it up and put it on their desk, and would also like a store-and-forward notification by email so that they can tell on arriving whether there was a problem. That produces two subscriptions: the secretary as Notification Recipient for the print-complete event, delivered immediately, and the submitter as Notification Recipient for the print-complete event with the impressions-completed attribute, delivered store-and-forward. In the third, the submitter is in one country and the client who will collect the job is in another, so the notification is immediate, for the print-complete event, with the notification language set to French.

The fourth scenario is a job sent from a hotel room to a print shop in the town the submitter is working in. An immediate notification would be of no use, so an email notification, sent store-and-forward, is chosen instead. The fifth is a large, complex file where the submitter wants immediate feedback on progress, with a subscription for all state transitions and the impression-completed attribute.

The sixth scenario is an operator whose duty is to keep the printer running. The operator subscribes independently of any job submission, so that the subscription outlasts any particular job, and asks for all Printer state transitions with the printer state, printer state reasons, device powering up and device powering down attributes. The seventh is a usage statistics gathering application, which subscribes independently as well, and whose subscription may persist across power cycles, and which asks for job completion with attributes such as impressions completed, sheets completed, time submitted, time started, time completed, job owner and job size in octets.

The eighth and ninth scenarios are client application programs that display a list of queued jobs, or a list of printers, with their current state. The window stays open for an independent amount of time and is desired to represent the current state, so the event delivery mechanism provides the means to update the screen on all needed changes, and the application only needs to perform a slow poll to recover from any missed notifications. The event delivery may also cover querying for attributes that are not delivered in the notification itself.

The last three scenarios are about IPP Servers that control devices. A server controlling devices that do not support notification or IPP at all has to support the IPP Notification semantics itself on behalf of each device, and in some cases must poll the devices to learn their job and device state and state changes so that it can send notifications. A server whose devices do support IPP Notification has a choice: forward the notification to the IPP Printers it controls and have them send the notifications to the intended recipients without its involvement, or replace the notification submitted with the job to indicate itself as the Notification Recipient, and then forward notifications to the recipients its clients asked for. A server whose printers may also be controlled by other servers wants job events only for the jobs it sends, but printer events all the time, so it subscribes to those printers for printer events with a long-standing subscription and itself as the Notification Recipient. When a job creation request arrives it also adds a job subscription for job events, with itself as the Notification Recipient, to the job's own subscriptions supplied by its clients. The memo calls this usage piggybacking. The IPP Printers automatically remove their job subscriptions when the job finishes, as for all job subscriptions, so the server stops getting job events once its jobs are completed.
sections.plainLanguage: The scenarios cover the obvious cases and the awkward ones. The awkward ones are: telling somebody else that a job is ready, telling a person in another country, telling a person who is not at their desk, watching a printer rather than a job, and a print server that has to speak for devices that cannot speak for themselves.

sections.title: Requirements for the Notification Specification
sections.content:
The requirements are intended to be met by the IPP Notification specification rather than by an implementation, and the memo says which of them are REQUIRED and which are OPTIONAL for a conforming implementation to support.

The specification must be designed so that an IPP Printer can transparently support the IPP Notification semantics by using third-party notification services that exist today or that may be standardized in the future. It must define a means for a Job-Submitting End User to specify zero or more Notification Recipients when submitting a print job, and a submitter will not be able to prevent out-of-band subscriptions from authorized persons such as Operators. It must define a means for a Notification Subscriber to specify one or more notification events for a Notification Recipient, subject to administrative and security policy restrictions.

The events that must be specifiable include any standard Printer MIB alert, Job Received, a transition from Unknown to Pending, Job Started, a transition from Pending to Processing, Page Complete, where the page is stacked, Collated Copy Complete, where the last sheet of the collated copy is stacked, Job Complete, a transition from Processing or Processing-stopped to Completed, Job Aborted, Job Canceled, other job state changes such as paused and purged, device problems for which the job is destined, and job (interpreter) issues.

The specification must define how an End User or Operator subscribes for any set of Job Events for a specific job, or any set of Printer Events while a specific job is not complete. It must define how an End User or Operator subscribes, without having to submit a job, for any set of Printer Events for a defined period, or for any set of Job Events for all jobs with no control over which jobs. It must define how the Notification Subscriber can specify either immediate or store-and-forward notification independently for each Notification Recipient, whether explicitly or implied by the method of delivery chosen by the Job-Submitting End User, and it must define common delivery methods, for example email.

It must define how an IPP Printer validates its ability to deliver an Event by using the specified delivery scheme. If the scheme is not supported, or is invalid for some reason, the IPP Printer accepts and performs the request anyway and indicates the unsupported attribute values. There is no requirement for the IPP Printer receiving the print request to validate the identity of a Notification Recipient, or the ability of the system to deliver an event to that recipient as requested, for example if the recipient is not at work that day. It must define a class of IPP event notification delivery methods that can flow through corporate firewalls, although an IPP printer need not test to guarantee delivery through a firewall before accepting a print job.

It may define a means to deliver a notification to the submitting client when the delivery of an event notification to a specified Notification Recipient fails, and a fallback means of polling for subscribers to determine whether notifications have failed. It must define a mechanism for localizing Human-Consumable Notifications by the Notification Source, and may define a way to specify whether event delivery requires acknowledgement back to the Notification Source.

There must be a mechanism so that job-independent subscriptions do not become stale and do not require human intervention to be removed, though a subscription must not be deemed stale only because it is unable to deliver an Event Notification, as temporary delivery problems must be tolerated. A mechanism must be defined so that an Event Subscriber can add an Event Subscription to a Job after the Job has been submitted, so that a client can cancel an Event Subscription on a job or printer after the job has been submitted, and so that a client can obtain the set of current Subscriptions.
sections.plainLanguage: The seventeen requirements say, in effect, that a printer has to let a client say who should be told, which changes should count as an event, and whether the message should arrive at once or be held until the recipient fetches it. A printer that cannot deliver a notification the way asked for still accepts the job and says which parts of the request it could not meet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo says the biggest security concern by far is the abuse of notification, that is, sending unwanted notifications to third parties, which is spam. The problem is made worse by notification addresses that may be redistributed to multiple parties, for example mailing lists. Scenarios exist in which third-party notification is required, and the memo points at two of them. The fully secure solution would require the active agreement of all recipients before anything is sent out, but requirement 9, which says there is no requirement for an IPP Printer receiving the print request to validate the identity of an event recipient, argues against this. Certain systems may decide to disallow third-party notifications, on the model of a traditional fax.

The same security issues are present when clients submit notification requests as when they submit an IPP/1.1 print job request, so the same mechanisms used by IPP/1.1 can be used for the client notification submission. Operations that require authentication can use the HTTP authentication, and operations that require privacy can use the HTTP/TLS privacy.

The notification access control model should be similar to the IPP access control model. Creating a notification subscription is associated with a user. Only the creator or an operator can cancel the subscription, and the system may limit the listing of items to items owned by the user. Some subscriptions, for example those that have a lifetime longer than a job, can be done only by privileged users, operators and/or administrators, if that is the authorization policy.

The standard security concerns apply to the notification delivery: delivery to the right user, privacy of content, and tamper-proof content. IPP should use the security mechanism of the delivery method used. Some delivery mechanisms are more secure than others, so sensitive notifications should use the delivery method that has the strongest security.
sections.plainLanguage: The main risk is that printing becomes a way to send unwanted mail, since a job can name somebody else as the person to notify. The memo does not require the printer to check who the recipient really is, because that would get in the way of the case where a colleague is asked to collect a printout. Instead, the printer applies the same authentication and access rules it already uses for print jobs.

sections.title: Internationalization and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The Human-Consumable Notification must be localized to the natural language and charset that the Notification Subscriber specifies, within the choice of natural languages and charsets that the IPP Printer supports.

The Machine-Consumable Notification data uses the application/ipp MIME media type. It contains attributes whose text values are required to be in the natural language and charset that the Notification Subscriber specifies, within the choice of natural languages and charsets that the IPP Printer supports.

On the IANA side, the memo records only that some notification delivery methods have been registered with IANA for use in URLs, and that these will be defined in other documents.
sections.plainLanguage: A notification meant for a person has to be in their language, and the subscriber says which language and character set they want, from the ones the printer supports. The machine-readable form of a notification uses the same media type as the rest of IPP.

viz.caption: THE WAYS A NOTIFICATION CAN BE DELIVERED

items.title: Immediate
items.text: Sent so that it arrives at once, within the limits of common addressing, routing, network congestion and quality of service.

items.title: Store and forward
items.text: Queued by an intermediate network application for later retrieval. Email is an example.

items.title: Reliable delivery
items.text: Delivered over a reliable transport with acknowledgement and retry. Guaranteed delivery needs both store-and-forward and a reliable transport.

items.title: Unreliable transport
items.text: Delivered through the ordinary transport and routing framework, with no acknowledgement or retry required.

items.title: For a person
items.text: Human-Consumable: intended for human end users only. A mixed notification contains both human and machine readable information.

items.title: For a program
items.text: Machine-Consumable: intended for a program such as an IPP Client, and may not contain human-readable information.

viz.caption: ILLUSTRATIVE: A NOTIFICATION REACHING THE PERSON WHO ASKED FOR IT

messages.label: EVENT NOTIFICATION
messages.note: When an event occurs the printer generates a notification that fully describes it, and sends it only because a subscription exists.

messages.label: NOTIFICATION
messages.note: The agent may act on the recipient's behalf, forward the notification by another means such as a pager, or queue it for later retrieval.

viz.caption: THE EVENTS A SUBSCRIBER CAN ASK TO BE TOLD ABOUT

items.label: Printer alert
items.desc: Any standard Printer MIB alert counts as a Job or Printer Event.

items.label: Copy stacked
items.desc: The last sheet of the collated copy is stacked.

items.label: Completed
items.desc: Transition from Processing or Processing-stopped to Completed.

items.label: Aborted
items.desc: Transition from Pending, Pending-held, Processing, or Processing-stopped to Aborted.

items.label: Canceled
items.desc: Transition from Pending, Pending-held, Processing, or Processing-held to Canceled.

items.label: Paused or purged
items.desc: Other job state changes, such as paused or purged.

items.label: For the job's device
items.desc: Device problems for which the job is destined.
